nameStory: Water Marigold gets its name from its bright yellow daisy-like flowers that resemble the cheerful blooms of garden marigolds, but this plant has made its home in the water. The 'Beck's' part of its formal name honors Lewis Caleb Beck, a 19th-century American botanist who studied the plants of New York and the Great Lakes region.
description: Water Marigold is an aquatic flowering plant that lives partially or fully submerged in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. It produces bright yellow daisy-like flowers that peek above the water surface on sturdy stems, while its finely divided underwater leaves create feathery underwater gardens. This perennial plant can grow 1-3 feet tall, with most of its leafy growth happening below the waterline.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with 6-10 broad petals surrounding a darker yellow center, held on sturdy stems that emerge above the water surface like little suns

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two distinct leaf types: feathery, finely divided underwater leaves that feel soft and delicate, and broader, more solid leaves above water that are opposite each other on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Semi-aquatic growth with most of the plant submerged, sending up flowering stems that break the water surface to bloom in the open air

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flat seeds with tiny barbs that can stick lightly to clothing or animal fur, typical of the beggarticks family

habitat: Look for Water Marigold in clean, quiet freshwater environments like pond edges, lake shores, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It prefers shallow areas where it can root in muddy bottoms while extending stems to the surface. This plant indicates good water quality and is often found with other aquatic plants like water lilies and pondweeds.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins underwater as water temperatures warm, with feathery submerged leaves emerging first from overwintering roots.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom from July through September, creating cheerful displays above the water surface on warm sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse while above-water portions begin to die back, though some underwater growth may persist in warmer areas.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to underwater roots and rhizomes, leaving little visible trace until spring growth begins again.

funFact: Water Marigold is like a plant shape-shifter - it grows completely different types of leaves depending on whether they're underwater or in the air, with the submerged leaves looking like delicate green feathers while the aerial leaves are broad and solid!
confusionNotes: Water Marigold might be confused with other yellow aquatic flowers, but remember: if you see bright yellow daisy-like blooms rising from feathery underwater foliage in clean water, you've likely found this special semi-aquatic member of the beggarticks family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Water Marigold isn't related to garden marigolds at all - it's actually a member of the sunflower family and closely related to those pesky beggarticks that stick to your socks on woodland walks.
compareHints: Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family. While other beggarticks have similar yellow flowers, Water Marigold is the only one that lives partially submerged with those distinctive feathery underwater leaves.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
